title: Written under obedience
hook: someone you love asks for something you'd never choose; Thérèse's sister asked her to write her memories
tomorrow: why would a saint be glad to be a daisy and not a rose?

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Francis de Sales's book with a clock, wound daily and cleaned once a year. The line was renew yearly. Now a new book, and a new voice.

Somebody you love asks for something you'd never have picked: record Grandpa's stories, make the slideshow for the anniversary, write down how the family got here. It feels like homework with feelings attached. A young French nun named Thérèse got a request like that. Her older sister, who was also her prioress, asked her to write down her memories. So Thérèse knelt before a statue of Mary and prayed for help. Then she opened the Gospel, and her eyes landed on one line.
screen: `A REQUEST YOU WOULDN'T PICK.` → `WRITE DOWN YOUR MEMORIES.` → `SHE OPENS THE GOSPEL.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims, Mark writes that Jesus, going up into a mountain, "called unto him whom he would himself." Thérèse reads it as the key to her life: not what she earned, but whom he chose to call. So her book, Story of a Soul, doesn't open on a birth date. It opens on that line. First, obedience. She didn't set out to write a book. Mother Agnes, her own sister Pauline, asked, and Thérèse said yes. In a Carmelite house a request from the prioress is something to obey, and she treats the writing that way: a small act of trust, not a project of her own. Second, the song. She won't tell her life in the usual way, she says. She'll sing the mercies of the Lord, borrowing the psalm: "The mercies of the Lord I will sing for ever." The memories are there to show what God did. Third, the flower. She calls the pages the story of a little white flower, and the flower is herself. Fourth, the reader. The pages are written to one person, the sister who asked. Here's the thing to tell a friend: a book Catholics still read began as a notebook for one sister.
screen: `WHOM HE WOULD HIMSELF.` · `SHE SAID YES.` · `THE MERCIES OF THE LORD.` · `WRITTEN TO ONE SISTER.` · then, large: `THE STORY OF A SOUL.`

segments.voice: Take a page and write one memory by hand, not a date, a moment you'd call a gift. If someone has asked you for a story lately, start with theirs. If you pray, you can begin with the psalm: the mercies of the Lord I will sing for ever.
Written under obedience. Thérèse began her book because someone she trusted asked, and she said yes.
Your line: the story of a soul. Not a résumé, a song of what was given. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics read Story of a Soul at home, in parish groups and in Carmelite communities, often slowly, a few pages at a time.

chat.meaning: Thérèse's book began as a yes to her sister's request, a small act of trust. A request from someone you trust can turn out to be a gift.
